options.reason: The annual death count directly measures how many motorists were killed in reported NYC crashes each year.
options.answer: Motorist deaths fell from 110 in 2013 to 81 in 2025 (26%), but this crash data has no miles-driven denominator and cannot show whether per-mile risk declined.
options.interpretation: This framing shows whether the annual number of motorists killed fell: it decreased from 110 in 2013 to 81 in 2025, despite fluctuations in between. It is a defensible count of the outcome recorded here, but it leaves exposure miles unanswered and therefore cannot establish a change in risk per mile.

options.denominator: Police-reported crashes in the same year
options.reason: Normalizing deaths by reported crashes provides a relevant crash-level comparison when the dataset contains no mileage exposure.
options.answer: Motorist deaths per 100,000 reported crashes rose from 54.0 in 2013 to 94.7 in 2025, so this crash-normalized measure did not decline; the data cannot determine per-mile risk.
options.interpretation: This framing answers how motorist fatalities changed relative to the volume of police-reported crashes: the rate increased from 54.0 per 100,000 reports in 2013 to 94.7 in 2025. It is defensible as a crash-normalized fatality measure, but reported crashes are not miles driven, so it leaves the per-mile risk question unanswered.
